source_text: Right, so this points to a whole class of problems that are not really "tech" problems, but, say, "economics" or "data analysis" problems.  Those could become part of a tech solution, i.e., if we understand a range of topics well, look at how they hook together, build a model of that, and then look for ways in which that model could run differently, we may put ourselves into a position to build a technical solution.  But that comes rather late in the game from a logical standpoint.  Here's an interesting example: my tech stack.  I'm using a Kinesis Advantage2 keyboard, but in the old days I was using a Kinesis Classic that I got around 2001.  The next thing in the chain is a Dell deck that allows the keyboard to talk to my phone.  The phone is a Samsung.  The next things after that are the OS and software like Termux that allows the phone to inter-communicate via 4G with the internet, from which it reaches Zone.  Now, that's a "technical" diagram, but you could also look at an historical diagram in which Zone's GNU/Linux Ubuntu system and the Android OS share some common heredity.  But my point is I guess a bit inspired by W Brian Arthur, which is just to say, these are not "random" assemblages of things at all.  Even just the keyboard I have been "carrying around" for 26 years, just without the high-powered server to connect it to, for example.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) I agree about the order. Understand the topics, see how they hook together, model that, look for ways the model could run differently, and only then build tooling. Most of the SF kernel starts at that last step. I've recorded this in the mission as §3.6 (`18c723f`), with your stack as the worked example.

🈖 ("inspired by W Brian Arthur") In *The Nature of Technology*, Arthur argues that a technology is a combination of earlier technologies. Each component is itself a technology, so the structure is recursive, and new technologies come mainly from new combinations. Your stack shows both of the diagrams that follow from this:
- **Assembly:** Kinesis → Dell dock → Samsung/DeX → Android → Termux → 4G → zone.
- **Heredity:** the Linux kernel shared by Android and Ubuntu; Kinesis Classic → Advantage2; ssh, mosh and tmux, all older than the phone.

The keyboard is the striking part. The assembly around it has been rebuilt several times in 26 years, and it stayed put.

㊭ (what that suggests for clients) For each client problem, draw both diagrams and ask **which component has persisted longest**. That component is the client's "keyboard". In the §3.4 cases it would be the paper invoice, the 200-page manual, the regulator's rule and the auditor's question. A tool that asks the client to drop that component will probably fail. A tool that builds a new assembly around it, the way your phone-plus-zone setup gave an old keyboard a powerful server, has a better chance. In scattering terms, the long-lived components shape the in-state before any new tool touches it.

🈳 (open) This also hints at why the economics and data-analysis problems come first. The long-lived components are often institutions rather than devices, such as a tariff schedule or an inspection regime. You can't see those from inside the tech world at all.

previous_reply_acts.text:
("an "abstract ontology" rather than a lexical one") Two ontologies now meet in the mission. The SVO triples are the lexical side: what people say they intend. The R-nodes are the abstract side: the factors any scattering passes through. The §3.1 fit joins them, for example delegate → R10, verify by a second process → R9, constrain spend → R11. The abstract side lives in three places:
- `futon3c/holes/labs/M-wm-wiring/wm-adjacency.edn` (the wiring matrix)
- `futon2/.../aif-equations.edn` (the 37-edge equation DAG)
- the R1–R16 pattern map

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("scales up to "the trade deficit with Mexico"") The three-scale table keeps the same rows (o, C, π/G, R11, R9, out-channels) at every size, and I think it bears out your claim of scale-freedom. What changes as you scale up is the C row. At the household level the preference is "hungry, cheap, now". At the national level it's food security against farm incomes against consumer prices, held by two governments and farmers on both sides. That ties back to §3.4, where the human problems sat where several parties' preferences meet. So in War Machine terms, the scale-free part is the form. The difficulty grows with the number of people setting R19 and how far apart they are.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (honest status) Using the R-nodes as an ontology doesn't need the wires to work. Using the War Machine as a *model* of a particular client does, and the PROOF-2a log shows the matrix at 104 wires with none verified live as of 09-26. I've noted that in the section so the two claims don't get mixed up.
